commentary_summary: Drewry's tonnemile index for Panamax vessels stayed elevated after surging last month, with a 13% rise YoY. | This is juxtaposed with the lowest inactivity levels in the Panamax segment after the end of Covid lockdowns, resulting in ample supply in the market, squeezing utilisation levels. | The tonnage underway in the East has reached historically high. With more than 20 mdwt laden tonnage already waiting at the anchor at the discharge ports in the East, the congestion is likely to exacerbate in the region. | Despite ample coal trade in the Asian markets aiding vessel demand, the Baltic P5TC rates have been on a downward trend as vessel utilisation remained subdued.

Drewry's tonnemile index for Panamax vessels moderated for the second consecutive week but continues to be elevated YoY. | The tonnage underway in the East moderated last week from its historical peak but the share of laden tonnage in the region edged up. | Tonnage of approximately 7.5 mdwt is waiting at the anchor in the Pacific to unload cargo, the highest level attained in 2024 so far. The surge in US' grain exports to Japan and South Korea from the US West coast has been a significant contributor to the heightened activity in the region. | Additionally, the laden tonnage waiting at the anchor in China has reached its second-highest level in 2024 so far as coal and soybean imports remain buoyant.

There was a slight increase in Panamax vessel utilisation, which rose marginally from 93.1% to 93.4% WoW. This 0.3% uptick is primarily due to robust activities in the coal market. | The heightened demand for coal in Asia, especially from China and India, driven by increased power consumption during the summer months, has significantly boosted coal imports. As a result, this seasonal surge in demand has led to a higher need for Panamax vessels, thereby boosting utilisation. | The laden tonnage at anchor in China has increased by 0.6 mdwt. This surge in congestion is attributed to substantial imports of soybean from Brazil and corn from Argentina. The influx of these agricultural commodities has resulted in a buildup of laden vessels at anchor, indicating heightened demand and seasonal peaks in import activities.

The Panamax vessel utilisation increased last week from 92.8% to 92.9%. However, the rise was marginal due to the contrary impact of change in laden and ballast speeds. While the global laden speed increased from 10.58 knots to 10.84 knots, the ballast speed dropped from 11.46 knots to 10.83 knots during the week, counterbalacing the impact on the vessel utilisation. | The tonne-mile index has risen significantly and reached its peak last week in 2024. The buoyant coal and grain trade continues to support Panamax demand, with the surge in the export of steel products aiding additional demand. | The tonnage underway in the East has been historically high in July 2024. With consistently strong coal trade between Indonesia and China, coupled with the surge in steel exports from China, Panamax demand in the region is high. The congestion at China's load ports reached the second-highest level in 2024 last week, indicating that exports from the region will rise in near-term.

The Panamax Tonne-miles index increased 7 points over the week, reaching 103. The tonnage at the port and anchor declined MoM in the East with more vessels underway, pushing up the tonne-miles in the previous week. | The rise in tonnage underway supported the firming up of freight rates in week 11. Utilisation also increased marginally in tandem with the tonne-miles index. | Laden tonnage at anchor dampened WoW for China due to a decline in seaborne coking coal imports, attributed to increased overland imports from Mongolia. | Conversely, laden tonnage at anchor in India inched up WoW after two weeks of decline, due to the country's increased focus on domestic steel production which could potentially drive up coking coal demand.

commentary_title: Panamax tonne-mile momentum accelerates due to robust soybean trade
commentary_summary: Panamax tonne-mile demand maintained positive momentum, rising 3.6% WoW in Week 26. This growth was primarily driven by stronger soybean shipments on the Brazil–China route. | Ballast tonnage in the Atlantic basin remained elevated, supported by the delayed soybean harvest in Brazil, which continued to fuel exports to China. Spot rates on this route rose by 9% in June, underlining robust demand. | Soybean exports from Argentina surged, doubling in June as suppliers rushed to ship cargoes ahead of the export tax hike scheduled for July. This further adds ballast tonnage to the Atlantic.

Panamax utilisation fell 1.2 percentage points in week 31 as the tonne-miles index weakened and Baltic rates softened; vessel capacity at anchor/port declined MoM as more vessels moved underway. | North Atlantic continued to ease due to muted demand and a lack of fresh inquiries, while South Atlantic stayed broadly steady after showing early signs of support that failed to sustain. | In contrast, the Pacific saw increased ballast congestion due to increased demand from Australia and Indonesia, followed by a new US–Indonesia trade deal reducing tariffs to 19% from 32%.

The Panamax market held a firmer feel overall this week with tonne-mile demand rose slightly 1.4% in week 47 to reach 109.3. In tandem, Benchamark baltic rates also followed this upward trajectory. | The USDA reported over 1.5 million tonnes of soybean sales to China last week, marking the first major purchase of the current marketing year, with shipments scheduled for two vessels, including a Kamsarmax. | Ballast congestion in the Atlantic is expected to edge higher in the coming weeks, supported by China stepping up US soybean buying and renewed demand from US Gulf grain and US East Coast coal trades.

commentary_title: Atlantic market leads gains in the Panamax market as coal demand supports the Pacific
commentary_summary: The tonne-miles index rose 2.7 to reach 108.4 at the end of week 39, with tighter available tonnage and stronger cargo enquiry in the North Continent and West Mediterranean lifting Skaw-Gibraltar transatlantic route rates to $20,380/day. Fronthaul demand was even stronger. | East Coast Australia round-trip rates also increased, while Indonesian coal activity strengthened later in the week, with an 82,000-dwt fixing via Indonesia to India at $25,500/day. A relatively less tonnage list helps owners to maintain firm rates. | China’s August coal production fell 7% YoY, extending the contraction to 14 consecutive months, while coal-fired power generation has continued to outpace domestic coal supply. This widening supply-demand gap could support near-term coal imports and Panamax demand, although softer coal-fired generation may limit the upside.
